Colour contrast for digital accessibility: thresholds, brand palette fixes and 12 traps

Published on 19 November 2026Reading time: 25 minutesBy the firm’s team

4.5:1WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11
RGAA criteria 3.1 to 3.3

Colour contrast is one of the digital accessibility failures most often reported in audits, and one of the easiest to fix, provided you know exactly what is being measured. The rules come down to three numbers: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and for user interface components, and 7:1 for the enhanced level. This article explains how these thresholds apply under WCAG 2.2 and the RGAA, how the ratio is calculated, how to correct a brand palette without betraying it (with calculated values), the 12 cases that catch teams out, and how to test a page yourself in half an hour.

What colour contrast measures, and who needs it

In digital accessibility, colour contrast is a ratio of luminance: it compares the perceived lightness of a piece of text (or a graphical element) with that of its background. The result is expressed as a ratio, from 1:1 (two identical colours, invisible text) to 21:1 (black on white). It is not a matter of taste or of hue: a red and a green of the same luminance give a ratio close to 1:1, even though they look very different to someone who distinguishes colours well.

This choice of measurement is explained by the people it protects. A person with low vision, an older person whose sensitivity to contrast has declined, a person who cannot tell certain colours apart, but also anyone reading on a phone in bright sunlight or on a poor-quality screen: all of them depend on the difference in luminance, not on the hue. A light grey on a white background, much loved in minimalist mock-ups, becomes unreadable in these situations long before it bothers the designer looking at it on a calibrated monitor.

Contrast is one of the fundamentals described in our guide to digital accessibility: it determines whether everything else can be read at all. It is also one of the few topics where the rule is entirely measurable. A criterion on whether a text alternative is relevant calls for judgement; a contrast criterion produces a number, which either passes or fails. That apparent simplicity hides a good many borderline cases, however, and the following sections go through them one by one.

The three colour rules you need to know
RuleWhat it requiresWCAG 2.2RGAA 4.1.2

Contrast of non-text elementsA ratio of 3:1 for user interface components and for graphical objects needed to understand the content1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, level AACriterion 3.3

The colour contrast thresholds to meet: 4.5:1, 3:1 and 7:1

Success criterion 1.4.3 of WCAG 2.2 sets level AA, the level required by every European regulation: text and images of text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with their background. For large text, the threshold drops to 3:1, because larger characters remain readable with less contrast. Level AAA, in criterion 1.4.6, raises these thresholds to 7:1 and 4.5:1; none of the texts applicable in France, Belgium, Luxembourg or Switzerland requires it, but it remains a good target for content intended for older readers or people with low vision.

Criterion 1.4.11, introduced in WCAG 2.1 and carried over into WCAG 2.2, extends the requirement to what is not text: the visual elements needed to identify a user interface component and its states (the outline of a field, the tick in a checkbox, the focus indicator), as well as the parts of a chart needed to understand it, must have a ratio of at least 3:1 against the adjacent colours.

These thresholds are minimums, not rounded figures. The W3C page Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3 states that values must not be rounded: a ratio of 4.49:1 does not meet the 4.5:1 requirement. This is a point that many tools obscure by displaying only one decimal place. Always record the ratio to two decimal places in your specifications, design files and acceptance criteria.

Contrast thresholds by type of element (level AA unless stated otherwise)
ElementMinimum thresholdReference

Large text (24 px and above, or 18.5 px and above in bold)3:1WCAG 1.4.3; RGAA 3.2

Key point

Three numbers settle the vast majority of design decisions: 4.5:1 for body text, and 3:1 for large text and for anything that is not text but is needed to understand or to act. No rounding: 4.49:1 is a failure.

Large text: 24 px, 18.5 px in bold, and the size traps

WCAG defines large text in points: at least 18 point, or at least 14 point in bold. The W3C notes that these values correspond approximately to 24 CSS pixels and to 18.66 CSS pixels in bold; the RGAA uses 24 px and 18.5 px in the tests for its criterion 3.2: the 4.5:1 threshold applies to non-bold text under 24 px and to bold text under 18.5 px; above that, 3:1 is enough. The official RGAA criteria and tests (in French) set out these tests criterion by criterion.

In practice, three traps keep coming up in audits. The first concerns the size actually rendered. A stylesheet written in rem or em does not state the size in pixels directly: you have to measure it in the browser’s inspection tool, using the computed value. A heading declared at 1.5rem is 24 px if the base font size is 16 px, but only 21 px if the site has reduced the base size to 14 px. The same heading can therefore count as large text on one site and as body text on another, with exactly the same CSS rule.

The second trap concerns font weight. Bold, in the sense used by the standards, means a typeface actually rendered in bold. A “semi-bold” weight (600) may look heavy in one typeface and light in another; a weight of 500 is generally not considered bold. To avoid any argument during an audit, reserve the 3:1 threshold for text of 24 px and above, or for text of 18.5 px and above at a weight of 700.

The third trap concerns responsive layout. A 28 px heading on desktop may shrink to 20 px on mobile through responsive layout rules. If it was approved at 3.2:1 on the grounds that it was large, it becomes non-compliant on a phone. Contrast must therefore be checked at every breakpoint where the size changes, not only on the desktop mock-up. The simplest safeguard is to note, for each text style in the design system, its smallest rendered size and the threshold that applies to it at that size.

Contrast of user interface components and charts: the 3:1 rule

Criterion 1.4.11 is often overlooked because it does not concern text. The W3C page Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.11 describes it as the guarantee that the elements needed to locate a component and understand its state remain perceivable. The RGAA includes it in its criterion 3.3, with the same 3:1 threshold and, as for text in criterion 3.2, the option of providing a mechanism that displays sufficient contrast.

Take a minimalist sign-up form: fields marked out by a thin grey #DDDDDD border on a white background. The ratio is 1.36:1. A person with low vision cannot see where to click, and the label alone does not tell them where the input area starts. The fix does not necessarily mean a thicker line: a #949494 border reaches 3.03:1 and is sufficient. Another accepted solution is a field background with enough contrast against the page background, if that is what marks out the area.

  • Form fields: the border, or the field background, must reach 3:1 against the page background if that is what makes the field identifiable;
  • Checkboxes, radio buttons, toggle switches: the box and the selected state (tick, dot, position of the switch) must each be perceivable at 3:1;
  • Buttons: if the button can only be recognised by its coloured background, that background must reach 3:1 against the page background; if the label is enough to identify the action, it is the text that must reach 4.5:1 against the button background;
  • Icons without text (menu, search, closing a window, basket): 3:1, because the icon is the only way to understand the action;
  • Charts: each series, bar or segment needed to read the chart must stand out from its neighbours at 3:1, or be supplemented by patterns, direct labels or a data table;
  • Focus indicator: the outline or visual change that signals the element active for keyboard users must also be perceivable at 3:1.

Charts are the most expensive case to fix after the event, because a palette of five colours close in luminance cannot reach 3:1 between every pair. Good practice is not to rely on colour alone to carry the information: label the lines directly, add patterns or different marker shapes, and provide the data as a table. Our teams build these rules into components from the design stage during an accessible development engagement, which avoids having to rework each chart one by one.

Information must never be conveyed by colour alone

Contrast is only part of the subject. WCAG criterion 1.4.1, included in RGAA criterion 3.1, prohibits conveying information by colour alone. An error message flagged only by a red outline, a required field indicated only by a red label, a map legend that contrasts green and red with no other cue: in all three cases, a person who cannot distinguish these colours, or who uses a screen reader, loses the information.

The most frequent case is that of links within a paragraph. A link that stands out from the surrounding text only by its colour, with no underline, raises a double problem. W3C technique G183 accepts this presentation on two conditions: a contrast of at least 3:1 between the link colour and the colour of the surrounding text, and an additional visual cue (an underline, for example) on hover and on focus. As the link colour must also reach 4.5:1 against the background, the equation is hard to solve on a white background with black text. The simplest approach remains to underline links in editorial content. The RGAA deals with this point in its criterion 10.6, which requires every link whose nature is not obvious to be visible in relation to the surrounding text.

Information carried by colour: common failures and fixes
SituationFailureSimple fix
Field in errorOnly the border turns redAdd a text error message, associated with the field, and an icon

How the contrast ratio is calculated, with two examples

The calculation is defined in WCAG from the relative luminance of each colour. Each red, green and blue component (from 0 to 255) is first scaled to between 0 and 1, then linearised: it is divided by 12.92 if it is low (below the threshold of 0.04045); otherwise the formula ((value + 0.055) / 1.055) raised to the power of 2.4 is applied. Relative luminance is then 0.2126 × red + 0.7152 × green + 0.0722 × blue. Green carries a lot of weight and blue very little: this is why a dark blue contrasts strongly with white, whereas a bright green contrasts poorly.

The ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the luminance of the lighter colour and L2 that of the darker one. With white (luminance 1) and black (luminance 0), you get 1.05 / 0.05, that is 21:1. Older versions of WCAG mentioned a linearisation threshold of 0.03928 instead of 0.04045; the difference has no practical effect on colours encoded in 8 bits.

Two examples show why rounding matters. Grey #767676 on a white background gives a ratio of 4.54:1: it passes. Grey #777777, just one unit lighter on each component, gives 4.48:1: it fails, even though a tool that rounds to one decimal place would display 4.5:1. The two greys are indistinguishable to the eye. This is why a brand guideline should set precise hexadecimal values, checked once and for all, rather than intentions such as “mid grey”.

Cases that distort the calculation

  • Transparency: a colour with opacity (rgba, opacity) has no fixed value; you must calculate the resulting colour on the actual background, then measure;
  • Font smoothing: the edge pixels of a thin letter are lighter than the declared colour; measure the colour declared in the code, not an edge pixel picked up with the eyedropper;
  • Gradients: measure the least contrasting part of the gradient that sits behind the text;
  • Background images: measure the least favourable area of the image, at each screen width, since cropping changes from one device to another;
  • Drop shadows and text outlines: a dark outline around white text can create the necessary contrast; in that case, it is the outline colour that is compared with the text and the background, and the outline must be thick enough to be genuinely perceived.

Brand palette: how to fix colour contrast without betraying your guidelines

Most contrast failures come from the brand guidelines themselves: a bright brand colour, chosen for a logo or a poster, reused as it is for links, buttons or small text. The following table gives colours that are frequently encountered, with their ratio on a white background calculated using the WCAG formula, and a darker variant from the same family that reaches the 4.5:1 threshold. These values are generic examples: run the calculation on your own colours.

Common colours on a white background: measured ratio and corrected variant
Original colourRatio on whitePossible use as it isCorrected variantRatio of the variant
Light grey #9999992.85:1Decoration only#7676764.54:1
Grey #9494943.03:1Field borders, icons, large text#5959597.00:1
Bright blue #007BFF3.98:1Large text, icons, borders#0069D95.22:1
Bright green #28A7453.13:1Large text, icons, borders#1E7E345.14:1
Orange #E65C003.56:1Large text, icons, borders#B347005.50:1
Light orange #FFA5001.97:1Decoration only; black text on an orange background possibleText #000000 on background #FFA500Over 10:1
Pure red #FF00003.99:1Large text, icons, borders#E000005.04:1

The most robust method is to break each brand colour down into several shades, each with an authorised use. The original shade remains the one for the logo, illustrations and large surfaces. A darker shade, of at least 4.5:1 on white, is used for text, links and button labels. An intermediate shade, of at least 3:1, is used for borders and icons. Reverse the reasoning for a coloured background: on an orange #E65C00 button, white text only reaches 3.56:1, but black text reaches 5.90:1. The button colour can therefore be kept if you change the colour of the text.

This approach also changes the conversation with the communications or brand team. The question is no longer “may we change our colour?”, which naturally meets resistance, but “which shade of our colour do we use for which job?”. The brand stays recognisable on every large surface, and the visitor gets text that can actually be read. Presenting the palette as a set of shades with their uses, rather than as a list of rejected colours, also makes the decision easier to explain to everyone who applies the guidelines.

  1. Inventory the colours actually in use by extracting every colour value from the stylesheets, then grouping them by use: text, background, border, icon, state.
  2. Calculate each planned text/background pair rather than each colour in isolation: the same grey can pass on white and fail on the light grey background of a callout box (#767676 drops to 4.17:1 on #F5F5F5).
  3. Break the brand colours down into shades by use with the verified ratio for each one and the list of permitted and prohibited uses.
  4. Translate the result into design tokens for example “text-link”, “field-border”, “alert-background”, so that teams choose a use rather than a colour.
  5. Document the approved pairs in the guidelines in the form of a simple matrix: which text colour on which background, at which size.
  6. Check again with every change because a new campaign colour or a new callout background is enough to reintroduce failures.

This work is done once, in a few days, and permanently resolves most non-conformities in the “Colours” theme. It becomes even more valuable in a component system shared between several websites: correcting one token propagates the fix everywhere. Our training courses for designers and developers use exactly this case study, working on the trainee organisation’s own brand guidelines.

Key point

Do not look for a single “accessible” brand colour: break it down into shades by use. The original colour stays on the logo and large surfaces, while a darker shade takes care of text and links.

The 12 colour contrast traps that audits report most often

The simplest failures (a paragraph in light grey) are spotted early. The ones still present at audit stage are almost always special cases, because they do not appear on the static mock-up or because no automated tool measures them correctly.

  1. Placeholder text in fields. It is often styled in light grey, sometimes well below the threshold. As it is visible text that gives an indication, it must reach 4.5:1; and it never replaces the field’s label.
  2. Hover and focus states. A button that complies at rest may become unreadable on hover if its background lightens. Each state (rest, hover, focus, active, selected) must be measured separately.
  3. Text on photographs. A white heading on a photo of the sky may pass on the right-hand half and fail on the left. A semi-transparent dark overlay or a solid band behind the text solves the problem for good.
  4. Carousels and background videos. The background changes constantly: you must check every image in the carousel, or guarantee the contrast with a fixed band under the text.
  5. Burnt-in video subtitles. White subtitles without a background become unreadable on a bright scene; an opaque or semi-opaque background behind the text is the safest solution.
  6. Banners and visuals with a slogan. Images of text are subject to the same thresholds as text; it is often the small-print legal notice at the bottom of the visual that fails.
  7. Struck-through prices and secondary mentions. Former prices, delivery information and footnotes are often deliberately toned down. If they carry information, they must reach 4.5:1, as our e-commerce accessibility checklist points out.
  8. Dark mode. Each theme must comply independently. A grey #757575, at 4.61:1 on white, only gives 4.07:1 on a dark #121212 background: what passes in one theme may fail in the other.
  9. Coloured alert messages. Green text on a pale green background, or orange on pale orange, often fails: you must measure the text against the background of the alert, not against the page background.
  10. Disabled buttons that are not really disabled. A genuinely inactive component is exempt. But a greyed-out button that remains clickable and displays an error message when clicked is not inactive: it must meet the thresholds.
  11. Removed focus indicators. A CSS rule that removes the focus outline without replacing it makes keyboard navigation impossible. The replacement must be visible and have sufficient contrast against the adjacent colours.
  12. Documents and emails. PDFs, presentations and newsletters often reuse the brand colours without any check. The same thresholds apply, as set out in our accessible PDF method.

The focus indicator deserves a further word. WCAG 2.2 added criterion 2.4.11 (level AA), which requires that the element with focus is not entirely hidden by other content, such as a sticky banner, and criterion 2.4.13 (level AAA), which specifies the minimum size and contrast of the focus indicator. These additions are covered in our article on the 9 new WCAG 2.2 success criteria. At level AA, the basic requirement remains that of criterion 2.4.7 (focus visible), combined with the 3:1 threshold for non-text elements.

What these twelve cases have in common is that they only appear in a real context: with real content, in a given state, on a given screen. A design review carried out on static mock-ups catches very few of them. This is why the test protocol later in this article deliberately includes keyboard navigation, hover states, error states, dark mode and mobile display, rather than a simple pass of an automated tool.

What is not subject to the colour contrast rules

Exceptions do exist, but they are narrower than people think. Criterion 1.4.3 excludes “incidental” text: text that is part of an inactive user interface component, pure decoration, text that is not visible to anyone, or text that is part of a picture containing other significant visual content (a street photograph in which a shop sign appears, for example). It also excludes logotypes, that is, text that is part of a logo or brand name.

Criterion 1.4.11, for its part, excludes inactive components, components whose appearance is determined entirely by the browser and not modified by the author (an unstyled native checkbox, for example), and graphical objects whose particular presentation is essential to the information being conveyed, such as a photograph, a heat map in which the colours are the data itself, or a logo.

Accepted exceptions and false friends
CaseExempt?Comment
Organisation’s logo in the headerYesThe text of the logo is a logotype; however, a slogan added next to it, in text, is not
“Submit” button disabled until the form is completeYes, if it is genuinely inactiveExplain elsewhere, in text, why the action is not yet possible
Purely decorative watermark textYesProvided it conveys no information
Legal notice in light grey at the bottom of a bannerNoIt is text that carries information, subject to 4.5:1 if it is small
Placeholder text in a fieldNoVisible, informative text
Checkbox styled by the siteNoAs soon as the author changes its appearance, the 3:1 threshold applies
Illustrative photographYesAn image does not need to have contrast, unless it contains text that carries information

Both the RGAA and WCAG provide for another route: offering a mechanism that displays a version of the page with sufficient contrast, such as a high-contrast theme switcher. This route is accepted, but it comes with requirements: the mechanism itself must be accessible and easy to find, and the high-contrast version must be complete. In practice, correcting the palette often costs less than maintaining two themes over time, and it benefits every visitor without any action on their part.

How to test the colour contrast of a page in 30 minutes

Automated tools detect plain HTML text on a solid background well. They miss almost everything else: text on images or gradients, hover and focus states, non-text elements, images of text, and content that only appears after an action. A reliable check therefore combines an automated pass with a targeted manual check, which anyone with training can carry out.

  1. Run an automated tool on the page to eliminate plain text failures in a few seconds, and note the items flagged as “needs review”.
  2. List the text and background colours present using the browser’s inspection tool, which also displays the calculated ratio for a selected piece of text.
  3. Manually measure text placed on images or gradients with a contrast analyser and its eyedropper, on the least favourable area, at several screen widths.
  4. Go through the page with the keyboard using the Tab key, to check that every interactive element displays a visible focus with sufficient contrast, and that no banner hides it.
  5. Hover over each type of link and button to measure the hover states, then trigger the error states of the forms.
  6. Check the non-text elements field outlines, checkboxes, toggle switches, stand-alone icons, charts: 3:1 against adjacent colours.
  7. Check information carried by colour by displaying the page in greyscale (an operating system option or a developer tool setting): any information that disappears is a failure.
  8. Repeat in dark mode and on mobile if the site offers a dark theme or changes font sizes depending on the screen.

This protocol covers the essentials of the “Colours” theme on a typical page. It does not replace a full audit, which checks the 106 RGAA criteria on a representative sample of pages and on the key user journeys. But it allows a team to deal with contrast failures before the audit rather than after, and this is precisely what we recommend in our article on how an RGAA audit unfolds. To make sure the fixes hold over time, accessibility acceptance testing builds these checks into every release.

Keep a simple record of each check: the page, the element, the two colours measured, the ratio to two decimal places, the threshold that applies and the result. This record becomes the reference for the development team when they make the fix, and the evidence for the next check. It also avoids a common waste of time, where the same element is measured several times by different people who reach slightly different conclusions because they did not measure the same area or the same state.

What digital accessibility audits check in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland

The thresholds are the same everywhere, because every national reference is based on WCAG level AA. What changes is the evaluation framework and the way the result is presented. To find out which framework applies to your organisation, our comparison of digital accessibility standards goes through the correspondences.

Colour contrast: applicable reference by country (November 2026)
CountryEvaluation referenceWhere the contrast requirements are found
FranceRGAA 4.1.2 (RGAA 5 is in preparation)Theme 3 “Colours”: criteria 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3; criterion 10.6 for links
BelgiumEN 301 549 standard (WCAG level AA)Clauses 9.1.4.1, 9.1.4.3 and 9.1.4.11 for the web; equivalents for documents (chapter 10) and software (chapter 11)
LuxembourgRAWeb for the web, RAAM for mobile, based on EN 301 549“Colours” theme, built on the model of the RGAA
SwitzerlandeCH-0059 standard, based on WCAG level AAWCAG criteria 1.4.1, 1.4.3 and 1.4.11
Private sector covered by the EAA (European Union)Requirements of Directive (EU) 2019/882, assessed in practice with EN 301 549Same clauses as for the public sector

In France, the French digital accessibility framework is assessed with RGAA 4.1.2, and a single contrast failure on a page in the sample makes the criterion non-compliant for that page. The future RGAA 5, whose progress we follow in our article on what has been decided for RGAA 5, is expected to align with WCAG 2.2; the WCAG contrast thresholds did not change between versions 2.1 and 2.2.

In Belgium, the evaluation follows the EN 301 549 standard directly, as presented on our page on digital accessibility in Belgium. In Luxembourg, the RAWeb published by the SIP applies the same standard using the RGAA’s methodological model. In Switzerland, the eCH-0059 standard refers to WCAG level AA. In France, Belgium and Luxembourg, the result of the evaluation feeds into the mandatory accessibility statement, in which contrast failures that have not been fixed must be listed as non-accessible content; in Switzerland, the federal administration also publishes statements of this kind.

For an organisation active in several of these countries, the practical consequence is reassuring: one well-corrected palette is valid everywhere. The contrast values you set in your design system do not need to change from one market to another; only the audit grid, the vocabulary of the report and the format of the statement differ.

What comes next? WCAG 3 and new calculation models

The WCAG 2 calculation model is criticised for a few known shortcomings: it sometimes judges white text on mid-tone colours too harshly and certain dark combinations too favourably, and it takes no account of size or weight beyond two levels. Other calculation methods, which factor in polarity (light text on a dark background or the reverse) and character size, are being studied for a future version.

None of this has any regulatory value today. WCAG 3 is still a W3C working draft, and its method for measuring contrast has not been settled. The European texts, EN 301 549, the RGAA, the RAWeb and the eCH-0059 standard are all based on the WCAG 2 ratio. An audit, a check by an authority or a public procurement procedure is judged on that ratio. The new methods can be used to refine an aesthetic choice, never to justify a ratio below 4.5:1 or 3:1.

Action plan: fixing colour contrast in four weeks

Contrast failures can be fixed quickly because they are concentrated in a few files: the global stylesheet, the component library and a handful of templates. The following plan suits a medium-sized website; it becomes considerably shorter if a design system already centralises the colours.

Four-week colour contrast correction plan
WeekActionsDeliverable
1Inventory of colours and text/background pairs; measurement of components and states; list of images of textMatrix of pairs with their ratio and status
2Breakdown of the brand guidelines into shades by use; approval by the communications team or art directionCorrected palette and design tokens
3Correction of the stylesheet and components; rework of visuals containing text, banners and document templatesCorrected version in the test environment
4Manual check of typical pages, dark mode and mobile; non-regression rule; update of the statementAcceptance test report and updated statement
  • Body text at 4.5:1 or more, large text at 3:1 or more, measured to two decimal places;
  • Field outlines, checkboxes, toggle switches, stand-alone icons and charts at 3:1 or more;
  • Hover, focus, error and selected states measured one by one;
  • No information conveyed by colour alone, and links in content underlined;
  • Text on images, carousels and subtitles checked on the least favourable area;
  • Dark mode and mobile display checked separately;
  • Brand guidelines updated with the authorised colour pairs;
  • Check built into every release to prevent failures from reappearing.

If your website must also demonstrate its compliance, an independent audit remains necessary: it measures contrast using the same method as the authorities and places these failures within the full set of criteria. Our RGAA audit for France, or our EN 301 549 compliance audit for Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and businesses covered by the European Accessibility Act, takes three weeks on average and delivers a prioritised list of fixes.

Frequently asked questions

What is the minimum colour contrast for website accessibility?

At level AA, the level required by European regulations, body text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text (24 px and above, or 18.5 px and above in bold) and the non-text elements needed to understand the content, such as field outlines or icons, must reach 3:1. Level AAA, which is optional, requires 7:1 for body text.

Is grey #767676 accessible on a white background?

Yes. Grey #767676 on white gives a ratio of 4.54:1, just above the 4.5:1 threshold required for body text. It is the lightest neutral grey that passes on a white background: #777777 only reaches 4.48:1. Be careful, though: it no longer passes on a very light grey background such as #F5F5F5 (4.17:1). You therefore need to check each text/background pair, not the text colour alone.

Does a logo have to meet the contrast rules?

No. WCAG explicitly excludes logotypes, that is, text that is part of a logo or brand name, from the contrast requirement. However, a slogan or wording written next to the logo, as text or in an image, is subject to the usual thresholds. Nor does the exception extend to brand colours reused for the website’s links or buttons.

Does a disabled button need sufficient contrast?

A genuinely inactive component is exempt from the contrast requirements, both for text and for graphical elements. But it must actually be disabled, and that state must be exposed to assistive technologies. A button that is merely greyed out and remains clickable is subject to the thresholds. Remember also to explain in text why the action is not yet available.

How do I check the contrast of text on an image?

Use a contrast analyser to measure the colour of the text and the least contrasting area of the image behind it, at several screen widths, since cropping changes depending on the device. If the ratio varies too much, add a solid colour band or a dark overlay behind the text: this is the most reliable solution, particularly for carousels.

Does dark mode also have to meet the contrast thresholds?

Yes. Every theme offered to visitors must meet the thresholds independently. A colour that complies on a white background may fail on a dark one: grey #757575 reaches 4.61:1 on white but only 4.07:1 on #121212. So measure each text/background pair in both themes, including hover and focus states.

Is an automated tool enough to check colour contrast?

No. Automated tools measure HTML text on a solid background well, but they cannot assess text on images or gradients, hover and focus states, images of text, or most non-text elements. They must be supplemented by a targeted manual check, which takes about thirty minutes per typical page for a trained person.
